The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge following an extensive search for a missing Port St. Lucie man. Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed the identity, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Michael Anthony Debevec was believed to have been wearing. Budensiek said a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, which led the family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Budensiek said there was a lot of decomposition, making it impossible to determine cause of death.

Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. Budensiek said investigators believe they found Debevec but could not confirm whether it was him.

hero.body:
A body was recovered Tuesday from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge in Martin County following a multi-day search for Michael Anthony Debevec, a Port St. Lucie man who had been missing since late August. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators believe the body is Debevec, though official identification has not been confirmed. Decomposition has made it impossible to determine a cause of death.

The search began Saturday after a Good Samaritan found a wallet belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, prompting his family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle that afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. The findings launched an extensive search involving detectives and ground and aerial units.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, searchers found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body.

Budensiek said the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. The sheriff said the level of decomposition prevents investigators from determining what occurred.

Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is imposing new restrictions on the use of automated license plate reader technology, limiting its use to forcible felony investigations and cases involving missing or endangered people.

 Sheriff Richard Del Toro Jr. announced the changes Monday, Sept. 1, as concerns continue to be raised across Florida about privacy, data sharing, government oversight and access to information collected by automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras.

 The Sheriff's Office said it will comply with Florida Department of Transportation regulations and directives governing license plate reader cameras located within state rights-of-way. Any agency-operated Flock cameras located on state roads or within FDOT-controlled rights-of-way will be removed in accordance with those requirements.

 Del Toro said his office will go further by placing additional restrictions on how the technology can be used within St. Lucie County.

 Under the new policy, use of the license plate reader system will require prior approval from the undersheriff. Searches will be limited to investigations involving forcible felonies as defined under Florida law and investigations involving missing or endangered people.

 The Sheriff's Office said the system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation or routine investigative inquiries.

 Access will also be restricted to personnel holding the rank of lieutenant or above. Use of the system will be subject to documentation, review and accountability requirements, according to the Sheriff's Office.

 Del Toro acknowledged that license plate reader technology has proved useful in serious investigations. The agency cited previous cases in which the technology helped authorities locate and arrest a homicide suspect, arrest a counterfeit currency suspect and safely locate a missing person.

 At the same time, the sheriff said access to powerful investigative technology should not mean unrestricted use.

 "Every search should have a legitimate public safety purpose, a defined approval process, and appropriate accountability," Del Toro said in the statement.

 The Sheriff's Office said it will continue reviewing Florida law, FDOT requirements, data-sharing practices, privacy protections and safeguards surrounding license plate reader technology. Policies will be revised when necessary to comply with the law and strengthen oversight, according to the agency.

 Del Toro also called for a broader statewide framework governing the technology. He said the Sheriff's Office supports working with the Florida Sheriffs Association, county leaders and state policymakers to establish consistent standards covering authorized uses, access, data retention, information sharing, auditing requirements, accountability and consequences for misuse.

 The sheriff said those safeguards should balance individual privacy and civil liberties with law enforcement's ability to use license plate reader technology during serious public safety investigations.
